newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity finishes down after new lows.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity finishes down after new lows.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures ended down after hitting new lows on cheap physical power prices and expectations of above-normal hydroelectric availability this spring, industry sources said.
Although most electricity deferreds recovered from new contract lows, traders said market fundamentals continued to be bearish for electricity.
"The daily trade prices are extremely low, they have a ton of water (for hydroelectric generation)," said one futures broker.

March California Oregon Border (COB) finished down 60 cents at $10.40 after hitting a new contract low of $9.75 and trading as high as $11.00, while April ended down 40 cents at $9.70 after hitting a contract low of $9.25 and trading as high as 10.00 per megawatt hour (MWh).
August and September, 1997, and January, February and March, 1998 COB also all hit new contract lows in Friday trade.

March Palo Verde (PV) settled down 59 cents at $12.70 per MWh after hitting a new low of $12.25 and trading as high as $13.00, while April PV ended down 28 cents at a new low of $11.80 and trading as high as $12.00 per MWh.
May and July, 1997, PV also hit new contract lows during the day.
Western spot physical power was said to be trading lower Friday, with Monday peak firm COB power assessed at $9.50-10.50 per MWh, while Monday firm peak PV power was pegged at $11.50-12.50 per MWh.

Separately, the Bonneville Power Administration requested that the WNP-2 nuclear power plant at Richland, Wash., run near half capacity through the weekend due to an abundance of cheaper-to-produce hydropower.

The Northwest River Forecast Center raised its January to July runoff forecast at The Dalles dam on the Columbia River in Oregon to 137 percent of average levels, a forecast which would exceed 1996 levels.
In the Pacific Northwest, rain and mountain snows were expected to continue in the area through late Saturday, with some drying expected early next week.

Temperatures in the Pacific Northwest were expected to average four to eight degrees Fahrenheit above normal into the weekend then cool to two to four degrees above normal by the end of the weekend and into early next week.
In the Southwest, dry and mild conditions were expected to continue through early Saturday, but rain and mountain snows were expected in western areas for Monday.
Southwest temperatures were called to run five to 10 degrees above normal through Sunday, then cool slightly for the beginning of next week.
NYMEX said an estimated total of 391 COB and 204 PV contracts traded Friday.
